title: Hackers Say They Won't Share Stolen FBI Data
summary:
Imagine someone got hold of thousands of FBI workers' private information — their home addresses, phone numbers, and social security numbers. That's what a hacking group called ShinyHunters says it did last Tuesday.

Now the group says it will NOT put that information online for everyone to see. But it also says it can't promise the data is safe. That's because it already shared a small piece of it with some journalists. The group says it can't control what those journalists do next.

ShinyHunters is famous for breaking into big companies and demanding money — called a ransom — to keep stolen data secret. But this time, the group says it never wanted money from the FBI. It says it hacked the FBI to fight what it calls false claims in an FBI report from May. That report said the group threatens victims' families.

The FBI hasn't said much about the group's latest statement. Ian Lin, a cybersecurity expert in Toronto, says the stolen data is still dangerous. "There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," he told CBC News. So even if the hackers keep quiet, the secrets may not stay secret forever.
why_it_matters: Kids share personal information online too, and this story shows why private details like addresses and phone numbers need to be protected — even big organizations can lose them.
